evidence_quotes.quote: By combining previously scattered historical, legal, and ethnographic sources, this article examines Australian Aboriginal dam and weir construction along the Roper River, focusing on the repeated re-purposing, re-contextualization and reinterpretation of the structures over time by both Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal protagonists.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 7, Study site, methods, and sources
evidence_quotes.quote: eighteen Aboriginal people and one non-Aboriginal former pastoralist were formally interviewed across ﬁve separate ﬁeld trips.

Holt took the matter to court in 1946, and the judge (Justice Wells) found in his favour and banned the practice. Despite the ban, Aboriginal cattle workers continued to construct similar structures elsewhere in the area until the 1970s, particularly on the adjacent Moroak Station.

As Thonemann made clear, the Aboriginal weir constructors on Elsey Station prior to 1945 had to await pastoralist permission before acting, and from 1938 were subject to both government permit processes and police interventions.

The most recent instance of the weirs relied upon the removal of some of the existing constraints, notably the return of ownership of the current Elsey area to Aboriginal hands and the formal resourcing of Aboriginal land management.

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative ethnographic, historical, and legal case study with no quantitative point estimates or statistical tests.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Customary Aboriginal seasonal weir construction in the upper Roper River was constrained by colonial pastoralist permission requirements, statutory permitting under the 1938 Water Ordinance, police inspections/removals in 1938 and 1945, and a 1946 Northern Territory Supreme Court ruling (Justice Wells) that eclipsed customary Aboriginal water rights arguments, invalidated the Administrator's permits on technical grounds, ruled the diversions unlawful at common law for diminishing downstream flow via evaporation, and banned unpermitted weirs while requiring government permits practically inaccessible to Aboriginal people. Despite the 1946 ban, Aboriginal stock-workers and cooperative pastoralists relocated seasonal weir construction to Moroak Station from 1951 to the late 1970s out of sight of authorities, and following restitution of Elsey Station to Aboriginal ownership in the 1990s and resourcing of the Mangarrayi Aboriginal Rangers, Aboriginal leaders revived weir construction in 2010 and research outcomes enabled formal government recognition of Aboriginal water management practices along the Roper River.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at ceiling 2 for a qualitative case study; primary court records (1946 Supreme Court transcript and judgment), administrative permit and police archives (1937–1946), and 19 formal interviews directly document how pastoralist permissions, 1938 Water Ordinance permits, police removals, common-law riparian litigation/injunction, and subsequent Aboriginal land restitution constrained, displaced, prohibited, or re-enabled Aboriginal surface water diversion and access.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 7, Study site, methods, and sources; PDF pp. 7–8, 12–18, Results; PDF p. 19, Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines colonial pastoral leases, British riparian common-law property rules, customary water rights claims, and 1990s Aboriginal land claim restitution (tenure, property); water allocation planning and formal recognition in the upper Roper planning area (planning); pastoralist permission requirements and practically inaccessible statutory water permits under the 1938 Water Ordinance (procedural_steps); administrative/police discretion treating damming as a domestic matter and informal pastoralist assent/cooperation on Elsey and Moroak Stations (discretion, accommodation); and downstream complaints, police weir removals in 1938/1945, and the 1946 Supreme Court riparian injunction, permit invalidation, and damages award (complaint, judicial_review, sanction).

outcome_flags.comment: Paper examines customary Aboriginal access to, retention of, and diversion of surface water in the upper Roper River and Red Lily Lagoon (for subsistence fishing/hunting, pastoral stock watering/irrigation, and wetland/erosion management) as well as downstream pastoral water access; no domestic utility connection or sanitation outcomes are studied.
